Part A · Chapter A4

Grading a model fairly

How to measure a model on records it was not fitted to, and what the measures can hide.

Accuracy on the records a model was fitted to does not show how it will do on new records. This chapter shows how to split the records into training, validation and test sets, average over folds and find leaks, then how to grade a yes-or-no model with the confusion matrix, thresholds, ROC and AUC. The last sections show when rare classes, base rates and subgroups make these numbers mislead.

You will need: the ideas of a model and a baseline from A1 and the logistic regression of A3, which supplies the scores graded here. From the toolkit: base rates, confidence intervals and reading a confusion matrix.

Overfitting and underfitting

Guess first. Fourteen made-up spadenose sharks give fourteen points of length and weight, and a curve with enough bends can pass close to all of them. Will it predict a new shark's weight better than a cubic, about as well, or worse?

A polynomial of degree M has LM as its highest power of the length L, so M = 1 is a line and M = 3 a cubic. Fitting finds the coefficients, the numbers that multiply the powers of L, that give the smallest training error for that degree. The training error is the RMSE (root mean squared error, the typical size of a miss in kg) of the fitted curve on the training sharks. The test error is its RMSE on sharks left out. A stiff curve misses the trend, so both errors are high (underfitting). A flexible curve fitted to few sharks follows the random scatter of their weights, so its training error is low and its test error can be high (overfitting).

  1. Navy dots are the 14 training sharks of the opening sample, the one shown on load, coral dots are sharks left out, and the teal curve is the polynomial. Drag M from 1 to 9: the navy training error in the right plot never rises, while the coral test error is lowest at M = 3 and then grows.
  2. Keep M = 9 and drag the training sample size to 60: the test error falls to 0.038 kg, level with the cubic's 0.037 kg.

In the opening sample the test error is lowest at degree 3 (0.039 kg); at degree 9 it is about 92 kg, while the training error is 0.023 kg.

How it works

Take the shark with tag number 3305, a 41.0 cm Sassoon spadenose of 0.228 kg that is not among the 14 training sharks of the opening sample. The degree-1 line predicts 0.234 kg, the cubic 0.224 kg and the degree-9 curve 0.262 kg, so the misses are 0.006, 0.004 and 0.034 kg. This case is mild. Yet inside the training lengths (18.2 to 49.6 cm) degree 9 is still worse than the cubic: its RMSE over the 222 test sharks there is 2.8 kg, against 0.035 kg for the cubic. Outside them it is far off, for example about 1,000 kg at 60 cm. So the 32 test sharks there account for nearly all of the squared error behind its test error of 91.6 kg.

91.6test RMSE at degree 9, kg÷0.0234training RMSE at degree 9, kg≈3,900times larger on the test sharks

Common belief. The model with the lowest training error is the best model.

Why it fails. Training error cannot rise as M grows, because a cubic is also a degree-4 curve (give L4 the coefficient 0). So the best degree-4 fit is at least as close to the training sharks. Choosing by training error therefore picks the largest M, even when the extra bends only follow the scatter in the weights.

Better account. Judge a model on sharks left out of the fitting (the validation set of the next section), and keep the model with the lowest error there.

Quick quiz

The training error is 0.02 kg and the test error is 0.30 kg. Is the model over- or underfitting, and what could you try?

Overfitting, because the test error is 15 times the training error. Try more training sharks, as in the figure, or a lower degree.

Why can the training error not rise when you go from degree 3 to degree 4?

A cubic is also a degree-4 curve (give L4 the coefficient 0), so the best degree-4 fit matches the training sharks at least as well as the best cubic.

Reading the figure

The opening sample is called Sample 2 of 12 in the figure and “the first sample” on its reset button. The coral dots are the other 254 spadenose records of the made-up catch table. At M = 1 the line cannot follow the bend in the data, so both errors are high. Around M = 3 the curve follows the trend and the two errors are close. At high degrees the curve bends to pass near the navy dots, and it swings far from the coral dots between them and beyond the ends. The weights of the sharks have a random scatter that does not repeat in new sharks. The test error measures how well the curve captured the part that does repeat. The sharks are made up: records generated from published length-weight relationships, not field data.

With 60 training sharks, a likely reason that degree 9 does about as well as the cubic is that more points restrict how far the fitted curve can swing. More data lets a model be more flexible before it overfits. Press "New sample" to see that the degree-9 curve changes a lot with the sample and the line much less. Across the 12 samples the line predicts between 0.06 and 0.11 kg for a 30 cm shark, and the degree-9 curve between −0.22 and 13.3 kg. Predictions from a curve that changes that much with the sample are unreliable for new sharks. Weight grows like length cubed (A2), so a cubic is a natural choice here. You will rarely know the right flexibility in advance, which is why you need a way to measure it.

Symbols

\[ \hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 L + w_2 L^2 + \cdots + w_M L^M \qquad \mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(y^{(i)} - \hat{y}^{(i)}\bigr)^2} \]

  • \(L\) is the length in cm and \(\hat{y}\) the predicted weight in kg. \(w_0, \dots, w_M\) are the coefficients of the powers of \(L\), the weights of the model, that the fit chooses, and \(M\) is the degree.
  • RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error (A2), so it is in kg. \(m\) is the number of records it is computed on: the 14 training sharks for training error, and the other spadenose records for test error.

Inside and outside the training lengths

Over the 222 test sharks inside that range, the cubic has an RMSE of 0.035 kg and the degree-9 curve 2.8 kg. Over the 32 test sharks outside it, the numbers are 0.060 kg and 258 kg. The degree-9 curve gives about 1,000 kg for a 60 cm shark, because no training point constrains it there.

Counting coefficients against records

Count the coefficients against the records. Degree \(M\) has \(M + 1\) coefficients. Degree 9 has 10 coefficients for 14 sharks. Degree 13 has 14 coefficients and passes through all 14 points, so its training error is 0.000. Its test error is about 850,000 kg (computed outside the figure, which stops at degree 9). A model with as many coefficients as training records can match them whatever the weights of the sharks are. A zero training error is then no evidence at all.

More data

More data moves the safe degree upward. The test error of the degree-9 curve is 92 kg with 14 training sharks, 0.055 kg with 30 and 0.038 kg with 60, level with the cubic's 0.037 kg. The test sharks here come from the same table as the training sharks. A new coast or a murkier season can differ, which is the subject of C3.

In practice

In practice, plot the training and validation errors against the dial you are tuning: the degree here, the depth or the number of trees later. Take the simplest setting whose validation error is close to the lowest. Fit polynomials on a rescaled length, as Polynomial.fit does in the code below. Raw powers of 49.6 reach \(10^{15}\), and rounding errors then dominate the fit.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Compare the two errors before you compare models. A low training error with a test error several times larger means overfitting: use more data, fewer coefficients or a simpler model. Both errors high and close together means underfitting: add a feature or allow more flexibility. B8 turns this into a full diagnosis with learning curves.

In Python

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")            # the made-up catch table
sp = df[df.species == "spadenose"].reset_index(drop=True)
L, W = sp.length_cm.values, sp.weight_kg.values

# shuffle the 268 records: 14 to train on, the rest to test
idx = np.random.RandomState(2).permutation(len(sp))
tr, te = idx[:14], idx[14:]

def rmse(a, b):
    return np.sqrt(np.mean((a - b) ** 2))

for M in [1, 3, 9]:
    p = np.polynomial.Polynomial.fit(L[tr], W[tr], M)
    e_train = rmse(p(L[tr]), W[tr])
    e_test = rmse(p(L[te]), W[te])
    print(f"degree {M}:  train {e_train:.3f}   test {e_test:.3f}")
degree 1:  train 0.046   test 0.057
degree 3:  train 0.040   test 0.039
degree 9:  train 0.023   test 91.566

More questions

A fit has 12 coefficients and 12 training sharks with different lengths. What training error do you expect, and what does it tell you?

Close to zero, because 12 coefficients can pass through 12 points. It gives no information about new sharks. Only the test error does.

Training, validation and test sets

Guess first. You fit four models to 600 made-up catch records and want to keep the best one. Would you grade them on the records they were fitted to? If not, on which records, and which records should give the number you report?

A split divides the records into three sets with different jobs, here 60% training, 20% validation and 20% test. Models are fitted to the training set, and the validation set is used to compare them and their settings. The test set stays locked until the choice is made, and its accuracy, taken once, is the number to report. The records are shuffled before the cut.

  1. Dots are made-up catch records, coloured by their set. The table gives the accuracy of four models, the share of species named correctly. Two of the models are decision trees, which ask a chain of yes-or-no questions about the measurements (for example, is the length above 40 cm?). The depth-3 tree asks at most three questions in a row, and the tree with no depth limit keeps asking until it fits its training records. Compare its training and validation columns.
  2. Press "Pick the best model on validation" (the depth-3 tree, 80.8%), then "Open the test set, once": its test accuracy, 78.3%, is the number to report.
  3. Press "Shuffle again", then pick and open again. The status line gives the lowest and highest test accuracy of your pick over 24 shuffles (73.3% to 88.3% for the depth-3 tree, plain 60/20/20 shuffle).
SplitShuffle
trainingvalidationtestringed: the 3 Ganges sharks

The tree with no depth limit has 100% accuracy on its training records but about 74% on the validation records, so its training accuracy overstates its accuracy on new records.

How it works

Take the depth-3 tree, which we pick because it has the best validation accuracy. It gets 78.3% of the 120 test records right, and that percentage is an estimate from a sample. Its standard error, the typical size of the error from using a sample, is \(\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\hat p\,(1-\hat p)/n}\) if the test records are independent draws. Here \(\hat p\) is the share answered correctly and \(n\) the number of test records.

0.783\(\hat p\), the share of test records right×0.217\(1-\hat p\), the share wrong÷120\(n\), the test records→ √ =0.038SE: 3.8 points

The shuffle starts from a seed, a number, and a fixed seed repeats the same cut. Another seed gives another test set, so the accuracy changes. Over the 24 shuffles of this split, the depth-3 tree's test accuracy has a standard deviation (SD, the typical distance from the mean) of 3.7 points, close to the SE of 3.8 points.

Common belief. If I use the test accuracy to choose between two models, it is still a test accuracy.

Why it fails. Choosing with the test set makes the winner the model that did best on those records, so its accuracy on them is somewhat too high. The more models you try, the larger the effect.

Better account. Choose with the validation set (or with cross-validation, next). Open the test set once, for the model you chose, and report that number.

Quick quiz

Why is a training accuracy of 100% no reason to choose the tree with no depth limit?

The tree was fitted to those records, so its accuracy on them says little about new records. On the validation records, which it was not fitted to, its accuracy is only about 74%.

You halve the test set from 120 to 60 records. By what factor does the standard error change?

It grows by \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4\), because the standard error goes with \(1/\sqrt{n}\).

Reading the figure

The trees are decision trees, which A5 explains, and the logistic regression is the model of A3. The task is to name the species from six measurements, with the models of the results table in 0.8, on the made-up catch records. The validation set compares models and settings, such as the degree in the last section. A shuffle puts the records in random order before the cut, and a fixed seed lets you repeat the cut (0.1). A stratified split gives the three sets about the same share of any one species. Across the 24 shuffles of the 60/20/20 split, the standard deviation of the test accuracy is 3.2 points for the logistic regression, 3.7 for the depth-3 tree and 3.6 for the tree with no depth limit.

A model whose training accuracy is far above its validation accuracy is probably overfitted, as in the last section. The model was chosen without the test set, so the test set has had no influence on the choice, and its accuracy is the number to report.

Shuffle again and the accuracies change, because the test set contains other records. A test accuracy is an average over a small group of records, so sampling noise applies to it. A test accuracy near 80% on 120 records has a standard error of about 3.7 points. Switch to the 80/10/10 split and the variation between shuffles grows, because the test set shrinks to 60 records. The standard error of an accuracy near 78% is then 5.3 points. Switch to 50/25/25 and the standard error falls to 3.4 points for 150 test records, although 24 shuffles are too few to show this for all models. The models are then fitted to fewer records. A split trades noise in the test accuracy against data for fitting.

Now look at the Ganges count in the three headers. There are only three Ganges records. A plain shuffle often leaves the test set with none, and sometimes puts all three in training. Switch to "Stratified by species" to deal the species out in proportion. With only three Ganges sharks even that cannot always give all three parts a share. At 50/25/25 the parts get one apiece. At 60/20/20 the test set can still get none, because a fifth of three is less than one.

Symbols

\[ \mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}\,(1-\hat{p})}{n}} \qquad \hat{p} \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE} \]

  • \(\hat{p}\) is the share of test records the model got right and \(n\) the number of test records. This is the standard error of a share from 0.7.
  • If the test records were independent draws, about 95% of test accuracies from sets like this one would fall within 1.96 SE of the model's long-run accuracy. The figure shows the interval for the current split.

The Ganges sharks in the test set

A random test set of 120 records leaves out all three Ganges sharks with a chance that is a product of three fractions:

480/600first Ganges shark is outside the test set×479/599second×478/598third=0.511chance of no Ganges shark in the test set

In 24 plain 60/20/20 shuffles of the table, the test set had no Ganges shark 11 times. That is close to the 12 that 0.511 predicts. A test set without a Ganges shark cannot measure recall for that species, and the same shuffle can put two or all three in training. The noise formula says the same in numbers. An accuracy of 0.78 has a standard error of 0.053 on 60 test records, 0.038 on 120 and 0.024 on 300.

In practice

In practice, 60/20/20 and 70/15/15 are common splits for a few hundred records, and a few per cent for the test set is enough when there are millions. With few records, choose with cross-validation (next section) and keep a small test set. A random split also answers one question only: how will the model do on records like these? If SharkCam will meet sharks from a different coast or season, build the test set to look like that place, for example by keeping whole dives aside.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Shuffle before you split. If the table is sorted by date, by site or by species, a plain cut puts one kind of record in the test set. Fix the seed so the same split can be rebuilt. And decide the split before you explore the data: anything you learn from the test records can leak into your choices.

In Python

import numpy as np

n = 600
order = np.random.RandomState(4127).permutation(n)   # a fixed shuffle

# 60 / 20 / 20
train, val, test = order[:360], order[360:480], order[480:]

print(len(train), len(val), len(test))
print("records in both train and test:", len(set(train) & set(test)))
print("first five test records:", np.sort(test)[:5])

More questions

A model gets 90 of 100 test records right. Give a 95% interval for its accuracy.

The standard error is \(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1/100} = 0.03\). The interval is 0.90 plus or minus 1.96 \(\times\) 0.03, from about 84% to 96%.

Cross-validation

Guess first. With 600 made-up records, the accuracy on a 20% test set has a standard deviation of three to four points between shuffles. How could you grade the model on all 600 records without ever grading it on a record it was fitted to?

In K-fold cross-validation the shuffled records are cut into K folds, slices of about equal size. In round k the model is fitted to the other K − 1 folds and graded on fold k, so its predictions for that fold are out-of-fold predictions. After K rounds all records have been graded once, by a model that was not fitted to them. The cross-validated accuracy is the mean of the K fold accuracies.

  1. Press Step. Fold 1 (sand dots) is left out, the model is fitted to the navy dots, and the accuracy on the sand dots appears in the dot plot. Step four more times: the five accuracies are 75.8%, 80.8%, 79.2%, 75.0% and 78.3%, with mean 77.8%.
  2. After the fifth step a table compares the models. The depth-3 tree averages 80.2% and the tree with no depth limit 70.5%, so the logistic regression, with 77.8%, ranks between them.
FoldsShuffle
Model
trainingfold being scoredringed: the 3 Ganges sharks

The logistic regression's five fold accuracies run from 75.0% to 80.8% with mean 77.8%, below the depth-3 tree (80.2%) and above the tree with no depth limit (70.5%).

How it works

Take the logistic regression on five folds. Let ak be its accuracy on fold k, found with a model fitted to the other four folds. The cross-validated accuracy is the mean, \(\mathrm{CV} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} a_k\), here with K = 5.

(0.758\(a_1\): fold 1+0.808\(a_2\)+0.792\(a_3\)+0.750\(a_4\)+0.783\(a_5\))÷5\(K\): folds=0.778CV, the cross-validated accuracy

The cross-validated accuracy is steadier than the accuracy on a single test set. Across 24 shuffles of the records, the logistic regression's accuracy on one test set of 120 records ranged from 72.5% to 84.2% (SD 3.2 points). Its 5-fold cross-validated accuracy ranged only from 77.0% to 78.8% (SD 0.45 points), probably because it uses predictions for all 600 records and not for 120.

Common belief. Cross-validation produces one final model that has been tested K times.

Why it fails. It fits K different models, and none of them is the final one. The accuracy therefore describes the recipe (the model type, settings and preprocessing), not any one fitted model.

Better account. Use cross-validation to choose the recipe. Then fit once to all the training records and grade that model on the test set.

Quick quiz

In 10-fold cross-validation on 600 records, how many records is the model fitted to in a round, and how many does it grade?

It is fitted to 540 records and grades 60. After ten rounds all 600 records have been graded once.

Cross-validation picks the depth-3 tree, with a mean of 80.2%. What should you fit and grade next?

Fit a new depth-3 tree to all the training records, then grade it once on the test set. The five trees fitted in the folds are not the final model.

Go deeper symbols, spread, model comparison, Python about 4 min

Reading the figure

The task is the species problem of 0.8 on the made-up catch records; seed 4127 gives the folds of that results table.

Switch the model and step again to compare. Press "Shuffle again": the individual fold accuracies move by a few points, but the means move much less than one test accuracy does, as the numbers above show.

Cross-validation costs \(K\) training runs, so it is practical for small data and fast models. Five or ten folds are common defaults. With ten folds the model is fitted to 90% of the records, which is closer to the final model than 80%. Use it on the training data to choose between models and settings. Keep the separate test set for one last, single check of the model you chose.

The fold accuracies in the dot plot are not independent, because any two training sets share most of their records. Treat their spread as a rough guide to the noise. For a formal answer about two models, use the paired test of 0.7 on the same folds.

Symbols

\[ \mathrm{CV} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} a_k \qquad \mathrm{SD} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(a_k - \mathrm{CV}\bigr)^2} \]

  • \(K\) is the number of folds and \(a_k\) the accuracy on fold \(k\), graded by a model fitted to the other \(K-1\) folds.
  • CV is the cross-validated accuracy. SD is the standard deviation of the fold accuracies, the spread from 0.7.

The spread of the fold accuracies

The spread of the fold accuracies is a number you can work out. Take the five accuracies 0.758, 0.808, 0.792, 0.750 and 0.783, with mean 0.778. Their gaps from the mean are −0.020, +0.030, +0.014, −0.028 and +0.005. The squares add up to 0.0023. Divide by \(K - 1 = 4\) to get 0.00058, then take the square root:

0.0023sum of squared gaps÷4K − 1→ √ =0.024SD of the fold accuracies: 2.4 points

Comparing two models on the same folds

Now compare two models on the same folds. The depth-3 tree beats the logistic regression in all five folds, by 0.8, 1.7, 2.5, 5.8 and 0.8 points. The sign test of 0.7 asks how often a fair coin gives five wins in five, counting either side: \(2/2^5 = 0.0625\). The folds share training records, so even that is optimistic. Five wins in five folds is suggestive and falls short of proof.

In practice

In practice, use 5 or 10 folds, shuffle first, and stratify for a rare class. For grouped data such as frames of one dive, use a grouped split. When two models differ by less than the SD of the fold accuracies, repeat the cross-validation with several seeds before you name a winner. If you also tune settings with the folds, the best tuned accuracy is a little too high, so keep the test set for the final number.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Shuffle before you fold, or the folds are slices of a sorted table. With a rare class, deal the species out in proportion (stratify), or one fold may contain none of the three Ganges sharks and its accuracy will not mean much.

In Python

import numpy as np

# ten made-up spadenose records: length (cm) and weight (kg)
L = np.array([22, 25, 28, 31, 33, 36, 38, 41, 44, 47])
W = np.array([0.03, 0.04, 0.06, 0.09, 0.10, 0.13, 0.16, 0.21, 0.27, 0.33])

def kfold(n, K, seed):
    idx = np.arange(n)
    np.random.RandomState(seed).shuffle(idx)    # shuffle first
    return np.array_split(idx, K)               # K nearly equal folds

scores = []
for k, fold in enumerate(kfold(len(L), 5, 4127)):
    train = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(L)), fold)   # all records outside the fold
    w1, w0 = np.polyfit(L[train], W[train], 1)      # fit a line on them
    err = np.sqrt(np.mean((w0 + w1 * L[fold] - W[fold]) ** 2))
    scores.append(err)
    ids = sorted(fold.tolist())
    print(f"fold {k + 1}: records {ids} score {err:.3f} kg")
print(f"cross-validated RMSE: {np.mean(scores):.3f} kg")
fold 1: records [7, 8] score 0.014 kg
fold 2: records [5, 9] score 0.044 kg
fold 3: records [2, 3] score 0.011 kg
fold 4: records [0, 4] score 0.040 kg
fold 5: records [1, 6] score 0.021 kg
cross-validated RMSE: 0.026 kg

More questions

Five folds give accuracies 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.80 and 0.80. Find the cross-validated accuracy and the SD.

The mean is 0.80. The gaps are −0.10, 0, +0.10, 0 and 0, with squares adding to 0.02. Divide by 4 to get 0.005, and the square root is 0.071. So CV = 0.80 with an SD of 0.07.

Leakage

Guess first. A model gets 95% on the test set, but one shark appears in both the training set and the test set, in different frames of a dive video. Is 95% still a fair estimate for sharks the camera has not seen?

Leakage is information from the test rows that reaches the model before the test. It can come through the labels (the correct answers), through preprocessing (scaling, filling gaps, picking columns), or through copies of one animal in both sets. The three tabs compare a leaky pipeline (all the steps from the raw table to a prediction) with a fair one.

  1. Switch between "Leaky pipeline" and "Fair pipeline" and compare the bars. In "Scaling" the two agree to within 0.2 points, so here the leak does no visible harm (its size depends on the model and the data).
  2. In "The same shark twice", navy squares are training frames and coral squares test frames of 12 made-up sharks. The first random frame split puts 8 of them in both sets. In the bars the tree with no depth limit gains 11 points and the logistic regression stays near 89%.
  3. In "Peeking at labels" the labels are coin flips, so the black line at 50% marks the fair accuracy. The leaky pipeline chooses 10 of 200 filler readings using all 80 labels before cross-validation.
Show

A random frame split raises the tree with no depth limit from 83.6% on new sharks to 94.7%, and peeking at all the labels turns coin flips into 74.9% accuracy.

How it works

Take the tree with no depth limit on 268 made-up sharks with 4 frames per shark, when the task is to tell mature from immature sharks. Its accuracy is 94.7% when frames are split at random, but 83.6% when whole sharks are split (means over 200 splits).

94.7%leaky test accuracy−83.6%accuracy on new sharks=11.1points too high

Suppose a random 20% of all frames go to the test set. A test frame has no sibling (another frame of its shark) in training only if its 3 other frames are also in the test set. That has chance about \(0.2^3 = 0.008\), so about 99% of the test frames have a sibling in training. A tree with no depth limit can fit individual frames, so a test frame whose sibling it was fitted to is easy for it, a likely reason for its gain. The logistic regression fits one smooth rule and gains little. A group split, with all frames of a shark in one set, removes this leak.

Common belief. Scaling, filling gaps and picking columns can be done once on the whole table.

Why it fails. These steps compute a mean, a median or a ranking of columns from the data, so done on the whole table they use the test rows. With labels involved the effect can be large.

Better account. Treat the whole pipeline as the model and fit all its steps on training rows only.

Quick quiz

Why does the logistic regression barely change between the leaky and the fair split, while the tree changes a lot?

A likely reason is that the tree can fit individual rows, so a test frame of a shark it was fitted to is easy. The logistic regression fits one smooth rule and has little ability to fit individual rows, so it gains little from the same shark in training.

You pick the 20 columns that best match the label on the whole table, then run 5-fold cross-validation. What goes wrong?

The selection used the labels of the records in all the test folds. Columns that match by chance look useful, and the fold accuracies are too high. Do the selection inside the training part of the current fold.

Go deeper symbols, duplicates, label peeking, Python about 5 min

Reading the figure

The definition of leakage follows Kaufman et al. (2012). A duplicate is the same row, or the same animal, in both the training and the test set. The sharks, frames and filler readings are made up, and the accuracies are means over 200 random splits. In the first two tabs the task is to tell mature from immature spadenose sharks from length, girth, depth, temperature and month. The 268 sharks have 4 made-up frames with small measurement errors.

Start with the first tab. A scaler computes a mean and a spread from data, so it is part of the model. If you fit it on the whole table, the test rows have influenced a number the model uses. Here the effect on the accuracy is close to zero for both models. That is no excuse to skip the rule. A leak can be harmless today and large next month, with a different model or a smaller table.

The second tab is the leak that matters for SharkCam. A dive video has many frames of one shark. Splitting frames at random puts the same shark on both sides, so the test frames are not new sharks. A model that can fit individual rows, such as a tree with no depth limit, can give a test frame the answer of its sibling frames in training, which share the shark's depth, temperature and month. This is a likely reason for its gain, because the figure shows the accuracies and not the inside of the model. The logistic regression fits one smooth rule and has little ability to fit individual rows, so its accuracy is the same either way. Treat a high accuracy from a flexible model on a split like this as a warning.

The third tab is the largest. The filler readings have no link to the labels, yet the accuracy is 75%. Choosing columns by looking at the labels of all the sharks, test sharks included, picks readings that match those labels by chance. Cross-validating afterwards cannot undo that. This is why preprocessing that uses the labels must be repeated inside the cross-validation loop, on the training rows of the current fold. In the language of sets (0.4), the training and test sets must have an empty overlap, and so must the information they pass to the model.

Symbols

\[ \mathrm{Train} \cap \mathrm{Test} = \varnothing \qquad \text{and all fitted steps see only Train} \]

  • \(\mathrm{Train}\) and \(\mathrm{Test}\) are the sets of animals (whole animals, and not single rows) used for training and for the test. \(\cap\) means the part they share, and \(\varnothing\) is the empty set.
  • "Fitted steps" means scaling, imputing, selecting columns and fitting. Any step that computes a number from data is fitted on the training rows only, then applied to the test rows.

Duplicates in numbers

For a shark with \(F\) frames, a test frame has no sibling in the training set only if the other \(F - 1\) frames of its shark also went to the test set. That has chance about \(0.2^{F-1}\). A dive video at 1 frame per second can give a shark 40 frames, and the chance is then close to zero.

Label peeking in numbers

The label-peeking tab is a selection effect. Take 80 sharks with coin-flip labels and 200 filler columns. A filler column has a correlation with the labels that varies around zero with a spread of about 0.11, which is \(1/\sqrt{80}\). The best of 200 columns reaches an absolute correlation of 0.33 on average in a simulation of 300 draws, three times the spread. Keep the ten best, and a model fitted to them reports a signal that came only from the selection.

In practice

In practice, put all the steps in one scikit-learn Pipeline and pass the pipeline to cross_val_score. The pipeline then refits scaling, selection and model on the training rows of the current fold. Split by animal, dive or patient when rows repeat. A column recorded after the outcome is a leak too. Ask of a column whether its value exists at the moment of prediction.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. An accuracy that is too good is a clue. If a simple model suddenly reaches 99%, look for leaks before you trust it. Look for duplicate rows, several rows from one animal, a column built from the label, or a step fitted before the split. Check the overlap directly, as in the code below.

In Python

import numpy as np

shark = np.repeat(np.arange(6), 4)    # 6 sharks, 4 frames each
rng = np.random.RandomState(1)

# leaky: split the 24 frames at random
order = rng.permutation(len(shark))
test_f, train_f = order[:6], order[6:]
both = set(shark[train_f].tolist()) & set(shark[test_f].tolist())
print("sharks in both sets:", sorted(both))

# fair: split the sharks, then take all their frames
test_sharks = rng.permutation(6)[:2]
is_test = np.isin(shark, test_sharks)
both = set(shark[~is_test].tolist()) & set(shark[is_test].tolist())
print("sharks in both sets:", sorted(both))
sharks in both sets: [0, 3, 4, 5]
sharks in both sets: []

More questions

A diabetes model uses a column "insulin prescribed", which is recorded correctly. Why is it a leak?

The prescription is written after the diagnosis. At screening time the value does not exist yet, so the model would be reading the doctor's decision back. Ask whether a column is known when the prediction is made.

The confusion matrix and its scores

Guess first. SharkCam's hammerhead detector flags 49 of the 600 made-up catch records, and 29 of the 49 are hammerheads, while the table has 57 hammerheads in all. What share of the hammerheads did the detector find: 29 of 49, 29 of 57, or 49 of 57?

Positives are the records the detector looks for, here the hammerheads, and all other records are negatives. A record gets a score between 0 and 1 from the detector and is flagged when the score reaches a threshold, here 0.30. The confusion matrix counts four kinds of answer: true positives (TP, flagged hammerheads), false positives (FP, false alarms), false negatives (FN, missed hammerheads) and true negatives (TN, other sharks not flagged). Accuracy, precision, recall (the share of positives found), specificity and F1 are ratios of these four counts.

  1. Dots are made-up records (coral hammerheads, navy other sharks); rows are the true class and columns the detector's answer, so the cell of a dot shows what happened to it. Click accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 in turn: a teal outline marks the cells in the numerator and a dashed outline the other cells in the denominator.
  2. Click recall: the boxes under the matrix show 29 ÷ 57 = 50.9%, the answer to the guess.

hammerhead (positive)any other shark (negative)teal outline: on top of the fractiondashed: the bottom (the top is included)

Click a score to see which cells it uses. Hover a dot to read the record.

Hover a dot to read its record.

At threshold 0.30 the detector finds 29 of the 57 hammerheads (recall 50.9%), and 29 of its 49 flags are right (precision 59.2%), while its accuracy of 92.0% shows neither.

How it works

Take threshold 0.30: TP = 29, FP = 20, FN = 28 and TN = 523, which add up to 600. The 49 flags are TP + FP, and the 57 hammerheads are TP + FN. Recall is the share of the hammerheads that are flagged, so it divides by TP + FN: 29 ÷ 57. Precision is the share of the flags that are hammerheads, so it divides by TP + FP: 29 ÷ 49. Specificity is the share of the other sharks that are not flagged, so it divides by TN + FP: 523 ÷ 543. F1 combines precision and recall into one number, and the figure below the equation compares F1 with their plain average.

92.0%accuracy: (29 + 523) ÷ 60059.2%precision: 29 ÷ (29 + 20)50.9%recall: 29 ÷ (29 + 28)96.3%specificity: 523 ÷ (523 + 20)54.7%F1: 2 × 29 ÷ (2 × 29 + 20 + 28)
  1. Guess a fair single number for a detector that flags all 600 records, then press "Flag all 600 records". Precision is now 9.5% and recall 100%, so the plain average is 54.8% but F1 is only 17.4%.
  2. Drag the sliders: F1 stays closer to the smaller of precision and recall than the plain average does, and it reaches 100% only when both are 100%.

Common belief. A detector that is 92% accurate finds 92% of the hammerheads.

Why it fails. Accuracy counts all 600 records, and most of them are not hammerheads. Recall counts only the 57 that are, so here an accuracy of 92.0% goes with finding 50.9% of the hammerheads.

Better account. Say which cell matters to you, then read its row or column: recall for the animals you must not miss, precision for the alarms you must not waste.

Quick quiz

Which measure would you watch if a false alarm costs the crew an hour, and which if a missed hammerhead is the worse outcome?

Precision for the false alarms, because it falls as FP rises. Recall for the misses, because it falls as FN rises.

A detector has TP = 8, FP = 2, FN = 12 and TN = 78. Find precision, recall and F1.

Precision is \(8/10 = 0.80\). Recall is \(8/20 = 0.40\). F1 is \(16/(16+2+12) = 16/30 = 0.53\).

Go deeper symbols, threshold 0.10, F1, Python about 4 min

Reading the matrix

The records are made-up. The scores come from a logistic regression on the logarithms of length, weight and girth and on depth and temperature. They are graded out of fold: a record is scored by a model that was not fitted to it. In this table the girth was computed from the weight.

The matrix puts the true class in the rows and the model's answer in the columns, as 0.8 shows. The 29 of 49 in the guess-first question is a different ratio from recall: of the flagged records, how many are right. That is precision.

Click the five measures in turn. Accuracy uses all four cells. Precision looks down the flagged column, so it counts the false alarms. Recall looks along the positive row, so it counts the misses. Specificity is recall's mirror for the negatives: of the sharks that are not hammerheads, how many were left alone. F1 combines precision and recall into one number. Recall is also called sensitivity, and in screening you will meet both words for the same ratio. The false positive rate is 1 minus specificity, and the ROC curve will need it.

Symbols

\[ \text{accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + FP + TN + FN} \qquad \text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \]

\[ \text{specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP} \qquad F_1 = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN} = \frac{2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}} \]

  • TP, FP, TN, FN are the counts of true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives.
  • Recall is the share of positives found. Precision is the share of flags that are right. Specificity is the share of negatives left alone. A ratio is undefined if its bottom is zero: precision when no record is flagged, recall when there are no positives.
  • \(F_1\) is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The two forms above are the same number, because \(\text{precision} = TP/(TP+FP)\) and \(\text{recall} = TP/(TP+FN)\).

A second case: threshold 0.10

A second case: the same detector at a threshold of 0.10. The counts are TP 50, FP 95, FN 7 and TN 448, and they add up to 600. Work through the five measures.

83.0%accuracy: (50 + 448) ÷ 60034.5%precision: 50 ÷ (50 + 95)87.7%recall: 50 ÷ (50 + 7)82.5%specificity: 448 ÷ (448 + 95)49.5%F1: 100 ÷ (100 + 95 + 7)

Compare this with 0.30, where recall was 50.9% and F1 54.7%. F1 is higher at 0.30 although recall is much lower there. F1 gives precision and recall equal weight. If a miss costs more than a false alarm, choosing the threshold with the highest F1 can pick the wrong one.

More classes, and in practice

The matrix grows with the number of classes. A five-species matrix has five rows and five columns. The row of a species gives its recall: the diagonal cell over the row total. The column of a species gives its precision: the diagonal cell over the column total. In practice, print the four counts beside the measures, and fix the main measure before you look at results. Scikit-learn's classification_report prints precision, recall and F1 for all classes in one table.

Why F1 and not the plain average?

The figure uses the made-up table. F1 is the harmonic mean, so it lies closer to the smaller of the two numbers. It does not use the true negatives, which is useful when negatives are plentiful and of little interest. That is also a limit: F1 does not change when TN changes.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Tools disagree on the layout of the matrix. Scikit-learn puts the true class in the rows and the predicted class in the columns, with the negative class first. Its matrix reads TN, FP in the top row and FN, TP in the bottom row. A swapped matrix turns recall into precision. Read the axis labels first, and check that the four counts add up to the number of records.

In Python

import numpy as np

# 12 made-up records; 1 = hammerhead
y = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0])
score = np.array([.9, .2, .6, .4, .1, .05, .3, .8, .7, .02, .55, .1])
flag = score >= 0.5                     # the threshold

tp = np.sum(flag & (y == 1))
fp = np.sum(flag & (y == 0))
fn = np.sum(~flag & (y == 1))
tn = np.sum(~flag & (y == 0))
print("TN FP / FN TP:", tn, fp, "/", fn, tp)

print("accuracy   ", (tp + tn) / len(y))
print("precision  ", tp / (tp + fp))
print("recall     ", tp / (tp + fn))
print("specificity", tn / (tn + fp))
print("F1         ", round(2 * tp / (2 * tp + fp + fn), 3))

More questions

A detector flags 10 records, and all 10 are hammerheads. Of the 57 in the table, what are its precision and recall?

Precision is 10 of 10, which is 100%. Recall is 10 of 57, which is 17.5%. A perfect precision can go with a detector that misses most of what it should find.

Moving the threshold

Guess first. The detector gives a record a score from 0 to 1 and flags the record if the score reaches a threshold. If you lower the threshold, does it find more hammerheads, fewer, or the same number? What happens to the false alarms?

A score is the number a model gives a record, higher meaning more likely a hammerhead (for a logistic regression it is a probability). The threshold \(\tau\) (tau) is the score at which the detector starts to flag, and a person chooses it. Lowering \(\tau\) removes misses (hammerheads not flagged) and adds false alarms (other sharks flagged), and raising it does the reverse. The best \(\tau\) therefore depends on the cost of a miss and the cost of a false alarm, which can be measured in time, money or harm.

  1. The strip shows the scores of the 600 made-up records, hammerheads (coral) above and other sharks (navy) below, and records right of the black line are flagged. Press "Threshold 0.30", then "Threshold 0.10": recall rises from 50.9% to 87.7% and precision falls from 59.2% to 34.5%.
  2. With the cost slider at 5 (a miss costs 5 false alarms), press "Jump to the cheapest threshold". The line moves to 0.168, where the total cost is 101, against 160 at 0.30.

Lowering the threshold from 0.30 to 0.10 raises recall from 50.9% to 87.7% and cuts precision from 59.2% to 34.5%.

How it works

Take a miss that costs 5 false alarms. At threshold 0.30 the detector makes 28 misses and 20 false alarms. The total cost is \(c_{FN}\,FN + c_{FP}\,FP\), where \(c_{FN} = 5\) is the cost of a miss and \(c_{FP} = 1\) the cost of a false alarm.

28misses (FN)×5cost of a miss+20false alarms (FP)×1cost of a false alarm=160total cost

For a record with probability \(p\) of being a hammerhead, flagging costs a false alarm with chance \(1-p\), and not flagging costs a miss with chance \(p\). The expected cost, the cost averaged over many records with the same \(p\), is therefore \((1-p)\,c_{FP}\) for flagging and \(p\,c_{FN}\) for not flagging. Flagging is cheaper when \((1-p)\,c_{FP} \le p\,c_{FN}\). Collecting terms gives \(c_{FP} \le p\,(c_{FP}+c_{FN})\), which is when \(p \ge \tau^{*} = c_{FP}/(c_{FP}+c_{FN})\), here \(1/6 = 0.167\) for \(c_{FN} = 5\) and \(c_{FP} = 1\). At 0.167 the counts and the cost, 101, are the same as at 0.168, the cheapest threshold in the figure. The rule assumes calibrated scores: records with a score near \(p\) should be hammerheads in about a share \(p\) of cases.

Common belief. A model has one accuracy, one precision and one recall.

Why it fails. Those numbers depend on the threshold as well as on the model, so the same model gives 50.9% recall at 0.30 and 87.7% at 0.10. For calibrated scores the usual default of 0.5 minimises the expected cost only when a miss and a false alarm cost the same.

Better account. Report the threshold with the measures, or report a curve that covers all thresholds, and pick the threshold from the costs.

Quick quiz

A missed hammerhead costs 9 false alarms. What threshold does the formula give, and is it above or below 0.5?

\(\tau^{*} = 1/(1+9) = 0.10\), below 0.5. When misses cost more, the detector should flag more readily.

Lowering the threshold never reduces recall. Why can it reduce precision?

Records flagged before are still flagged, so TP cannot fall, and recall cannot fall. The extra flags may be mostly other sharks, so FP can grow faster than TP and precision can fall.
