Reading the figure

Records outlined in black are errors. Drag the line or use the slider, and watch the dot move along the ROC curve, which the next section explains. The records are made-up, not field data.

Hammerheads (coral, top lane) mostly score higher than other sharks (navy, bottom lane), but the lanes overlap, so no threshold separates them cleanly. The matrix, the five measures and the dot on the ROC curve all follow the line. The horizontal axis is the score drawn on a log-odds scale, as in A3, so that the many low scores spread out; the labels give the probabilities.

The right threshold depends on what the two errors cost. Say a missed hammerhead is five times as bad as a false alarm. The scalloped hammerhead is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, so a crew that misses one could keep an animal it should have released. A false alarm costs a short stop. Set the cost slider to 5. The sand curve under the strip adds up the errors for the different thresholds, and its lowest point is the cheapest. If the scores are well calibrated, the short calculation below gives that point directly.

With a cost of 5 the formula (0.167) and the cheapest threshold on these records (0.168) agree to two decimals. Try 10 or 20, and they drift apart. The formula assumes the probabilities are well calibrated, and a model can rank records well and still give probabilities that are too high or too low. The cost curve is also flat near its bottom, so several thresholds cost almost the same. Choose the threshold on validation scores (or on out-of-fold scores, as here), freeze it, and only then open the test set.

Symbols

\[ \text{cost} = c_{FN}\,FN + c_{FP}\,FP \qquad \text{flag when } p \ge \tau^{*} = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}} \]

  • \(c_{FN}\) and \(c_{FP}\) are the cost of one miss and one false alarm, in any unit you choose. Only their ratio matters.
  • \(p\) is the model's probability for a record and \(\tau^{*}\) the threshold that minimises the expected cost, assuming \(p\) is calibrated. With a miss costing 5 false alarms, \(\tau^{*} = 1/6 = 0.167\).

The algebra in steps

The rule follows from a few lines of algebra. Flagging a record pays for a false alarm with chance \(1 - p\), so its expected cost is \((1-p)\,c_{FP}\). Leaving it alone pays for a miss with chance \(p\), so its expected cost is \(p\,c_{FN}\). Flag when the first is smaller: \((1-p)\,c_{FP} \le p\,c_{FN}\). Collect the terms: \(c_{FP} \le p\,(c_{FN} + c_{FP})\). Divide, and \(p \ge c_{FP}/(c_{FP}+c_{FN})\).

Checking the rule on the table

Now check it on the table, with a miss costing 5. The cost is \(5\,FN + FP\) at a threshold:

thresholdTPFPFNcost
0.50191238202
0.30292028160
0.167 (1/6)475110101
0.1050957130
0.05541883203

Made-up records, out-of-fold scores. Cost = 5 × FN + FP.

The cheapest row is the one at 1/6. Going from 0.30 to 0.10 finds 21 more hammerheads and adds 75 more false alarms, which is 3.6 false alarms per hammerhead found. That is below the price of a miss, so the move lowers the cost. Going on to 0.05 finds 4 more and adds 93, which is 23 false alarms per hammerhead, far above 5. The cost rises again.

In practice

In practice, the rule is often a target, such as "find at least 90% of the hammerheads". Take the highest threshold on validation scores that reaches the target. Here it is 0.0847, with 52 hammerheads found (91%), 118 false alarms and a precision of 31%. State the price of the target. Check the threshold again when the base rate or the water changes, because a threshold is tied to the population it was chosen on.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If recall looks too low, check the threshold before you retrain. A model trained on a rare class often gives low probabilities to all its records, so the default threshold of 0.5 flags almost no records. Lower the threshold on validation data and look again.

In Python

import numpy as np

# the same 12 made-up records
y = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0])
score = np.array([.9, .2, .6, .4, .1, .05, .3, .8, .7, .02, .55, .1])

for tau in [0.7, 0.5, 0.35, 0.15]:
    flag = score >= tau
    tp = np.sum(flag & (y == 1))
    fp = np.sum(flag & (y == 0))
    fn = np.sum(~flag & (y == 1))
    print(f"threshold {tau:.2f}: flags {flag.sum():2d}"
          f"   recall {tp / (tp + fn):.2f}   precision {tp / (tp + fp):.2f}")
threshold 0.70: flags  3   recall 0.50   precision 0.67
threshold 0.50: flags  5   recall 0.75   precision 0.60
threshold 0.35: flags  6   recall 1.00   precision 0.67
threshold 0.15: flags  8   recall 1.00   precision 0.50

More questions

Lowering the threshold from 0.10 to 0.05 finds 4 more hammerheads (50 to 54) and adds 93 false alarms (95 to 188). Is it worth it if a miss costs 5 false alarms?

That is 93/4, about 23 false alarms per extra hammerhead, against a break-even of 5. The move does not pay. The total cost rises from 130 to 203.

The ROC curve and AUC

Guess first. Pick one hammerhead and one other shark at random from the made-up catch table. How often will the hammerhead have the higher score, if the scores are no better than coin flips? And if they are perfect?

The true positive rate (TPR) is the share of positives flagged, the same number as recall. The false positive rate (FPR) is the share of negatives flagged, which is 1 minus specificity. A ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve plots TPR against FPR as the threshold moves from high to low, so it shows all thresholds in one curve. Its area, the AUC (area under the curve), equals the chance that a random positive scores above a random negative, with ties (two records with the same score) counting half.

  1. Choose a scorer ("Five measurements" is a logistic regression on length, weight, girth, water depth and temperature) and drag the threshold slider from right to left. The coral dot climbs when it passes a hammerhead and moves right when it passes another shark. "Coin flip" follows the dashed diagonal, with AUC 0.509.
  2. Press "Draw 100 pairs" a few times. A draw compares a random hammerhead with a random other shark, and the share of draws in which the hammerhead scores higher moves towards 92%. "Check all pairs" gives the AUC itself, 0.920.
Scores from

The five-measurement scorer has an AUC of 0.920 (the hammerhead scores higher in 28,467 of 30,951 pairs), against 0.802 for length alone and about 0.5 for a coin flip.

How it works

Take eight records with scores 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1, of which 0.9, 0.7 and 0.4 are positive. There are 3 × 5 = 15 pairs of one positive and one negative. The positive 0.9 outscores all 5 negatives, 0.7 outscores 4 (all but 0.8) and 0.4 outscores 3 (the negatives 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1). The positive therefore scores higher in 12 of the 15 pairs.

12pairs where the positive scores higher: 5 + 4 + 3÷15pairs: 3 positives × 5 negatives=0.8AUC

Common belief. An AUC of 0.92 means the model is right 92% of the time.

Why it fails. Accuracy needs a threshold and counts all records, whereas AUC compares positives with negatives over all thresholds. The same model has an AUC of 0.920 and an accuracy of 83.0% at threshold 0.10. The AUC does not give the false positive rate or the precision at the threshold you will use, because it summarises all thresholds. Precision also depends on the base rate, the share of positives.

Better account. AUC measures how well the scores order the records, but you still need a threshold, chosen from the costs, to turn scores into decisions.

Quick quiz

What AUC would you expect from scores that are random and unrelated to the labels, and what from scores that are perfectly upside down?

About 0.5 for random scores. About 0 for upside-down scores: the positive nearly always scores lower, so reversing the sign gives about 1.

Does the AUC change if you double the number of negatives by adding more records of the same kind?

Not in expectation. AUC compares a positive with a negative, so the mix of the data does not matter, as long as the new negatives are like the old ones. Precision at a fixed threshold would fall.

Go deeper symbols, ROC path, bootstrap, practice, Python about 5 min

Reading the figure

ROC is short for receiver operating characteristic, a name from radar (Fawcett, 2006). The AUC is a number from 0 to 1. The records are made-up, and the scores are out-of-fold.

Read the curve from the bottom left. A threshold above all the scores flags no record, which puts you at (0, 0). A scorer that ranks well climbs steeply before it moves right, so its curve runs close to the top left corner.

A draw picks a random hammerhead and a random other shark and checks which has the higher score, and “Check all pairs” runs through all of them. This is why AUC has a plain meaning (Hanley and McNeil, 1982): it is the chance that the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. It does not depend on one threshold, and it does not depend on how common the positives are, because it compares positives only with negatives.

What AUC does not tell you

The fact that AUC does not depend on how common the positives are is a strength and a limit. A model with an AUC of 0.92 ranks well. It does not give the false positive rate or the precision at the threshold you pick, because AUC summarises all thresholds, and precision also depends on the base rate. The next sections come back to this. An AUC below 0.5 means the scores are upside down, so flipping the sign of the score would help.

The hammerhead scorer in pairs

For the scorer of the figure, the pair count gives the same AUC as the area under the curve:

28,468.5pairs ranked right: 28,467 wins + half of 3 ties÷30,95157 hammerheads × 543 others=0.920AUC

Symbols

\[ \mathrm{TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \qquad \mathrm{FPR} = \frac{FP}{FP + TN} \qquad \mathrm{AUC} = \frac{1}{n_{+}\,n_{-}} \sum_{i \in \text{pos}} \sum_{j \in \text{neg}} \Bigl[\mathbf{1}(s_i > s_j) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}(s_i = s_j)\Bigr] \]

  • TPR is recall, and FPR is 1 minus specificity. The ROC curve plots one against the other for all thresholds.
  • \(n_{+}\) and \(n_{-}\) are the numbers of positives and negatives, and \(s_i\) is the score of record \(i\). The sums run over all pairs of one positive and one negative. \(\mathbf{1}(\cdot)\) is 1 if the statement inside is true and 0 if not.

The eight records and the ROC path

For the eight records of the worked example above, lower the threshold past one score at a time. A positive moves the dot up by 1/3, and a negative moves it right by 1/5. The path runs (0, 0), (0, 1/3), (1/5, 1/3), (1/5, 2/3), (2/5, 2/3), (2/5, 1), and then straight right to (1, 1).

The area under this path is a sum of strips. A step to the right has width 1/5 and adds a strip as tall as the dot is high. The first negative is passed at height 1/3, the second at 2/3, and the last three at height 1. The height is the share of positives that outscore that negative.

41/3 + 2/3 + 1 + 1 + 1: share of positives above that negative, added up÷5negatives=0.8AUC

This is the pair count of the code below in another order: 12 wins in 15 pairs is also 0.8. How uncertain is the 0.920 of the hammerhead scorer? A simulation can show. Draw 600 of the scored records with repeats, compute the AUC, and do this 2,000 times. The middle 95% of those AUCs runs from 0.884 to 0.951.

In practice

AUC also averages over thresholds you would never use. At a false positive rate no higher than 5%, the scorer finds 59.6% of the hammerheads. At no higher than 10% it finds 82.5%. Two scorers with the same AUC can differ in that region. In practice, quote the AUC with an interval, and add the true positive rate at the false alarm rate you can afford.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If you get an AUC well below 0.5, the sign of the score or the labelling of the positive class is probably flipped. If you get an AUC of 1.0 on a new dataset, suspect a leak (earlier in this chapter) before you suspect a perfect model.

In Python

import numpy as np

# 8 made-up records: 3 positives, 5 negatives
y = np.array([1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])
s = np.array([.9, .7, .4, .8, .5, .3, .2, .1])

pos, neg = s[y == 1], s[y == 0]
# every positive against every negative
wins = (pos[:, None] > neg[None, :]).sum()
ties = (pos[:, None] == neg[None, :]).sum()
pairs = len(pos) * len(neg)
print("AUC from pairs:", (wins + 0.5 * ties) / pairs)

# the same number from the ROC curve: sort by score,
# step up for a positive or right for a negative, add trapezoids
order = np.argsort(-s)
tpr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(y[order]) / y.sum()])
fpr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(1 - y[order]) / (1 - y).sum()])
area = np.sum((fpr[1:] - fpr[:-1]) * (tpr[1:] + tpr[:-1]) / 2)
print("AUC from curve:", area)
AUC from pairs: 0.8
AUC from curve: 0.8

More questions

Two positives score 0.9 and 0.4. Three negatives score 0.6, 0.3 and 0.2. What is the AUC?

There are 6 pairs. The 0.9 beats all three negatives. The 0.4 beats 0.3 and 0.2 and loses to 0.6. That is 5 wins in 6 pairs, an AUC of 0.83.

Rare classes

Guess first. The made-up catch table has 600 records, and 3 of them are Ganges sharks. A model that never says "Ganges" gets 597 of the 600 right. What is its accuracy, and how many Ganges sharks does it find?

A rare class has few records: the Ganges shark is 3 of the 600, a base rate (share of the records) of 0.5%. The lazy model never flags the positive class, so its accuracy is the share of negatives, 99.5% here. When one class is rare, most right answers are for the common class, so accuracy mostly measures the common class. Recall and precision for the rare class show more than accuracy does about whether a model is useful, because both are computed for the rare class. The precision-recall (PR) curve plots precision against recall as the threshold moves from high to low. Its dashed floor is random flagging, which flags records at random and so has a precision equal to the base rate.

  1. Choose "Never flags" for the Ganges class: accuracy is 99.5% and recall 0%. "Flags all records" gives recall 100% and precision 0.5%, the base rate.
  2. Choose "Logistic regression" at threshold 0.10: it finds all 3 Ganges sharks with 4 false alarms, so recall is 100%, precision 42.9% and accuracy 99.3%, below the lazy model's 99.5%.
ClassModel
positive record (flagged or not)all other recordsringed: flagged by the model

A model that never flags a Ganges shark has 99.5% accuracy and finds none, while one that finds all three at threshold 0.10 has 4 false alarms and 99.3% accuracy.

How it works

Take the lazy model on the Ganges class. It flags no record, so its 597 right calls are the negatives, and none of the 3 Ganges sharks is found.

597right calls: all negatives÷600records=99.5%accuracyand0Ganges sharks found÷3Ganges sharks=0%recall

A ROC curve can look excellent for the same task. For the Ganges class the logistic regression has an AUC of 0.997. At the threshold that finds all three sharks its false positive rate is only 4 of 597, or 0.7%. Its precision is 3 of 7, or 43%. Precision divides by the 7 flagged records and the false positive rate by the 597 negatives, so the same 4 false alarms weigh differently.

Common belief. A model that is 99.5% accurate works.

Why it fails. A model that flags no record is 99.5% accurate on the same table. Accuracy adds up the correct answers, and the 597 common records dominate the sum.

Better account. Compare with the lazy baseline before you trust an accuracy. Then read recall and precision for the rare class, with an interval that shows how few records lie behind them.

Quick quiz

A model flags 7 records and finds all 3 Ganges sharks. What are its precision, recall and accuracy?

Precision is 3 of 7, 43%. Recall is 3 of 3, 100%. It makes 4 false alarms, so 596 of the 600 calls are right: accuracy 99.3%, which is below the 99.5% of the lazy model.

Why can a ROC curve look excellent when the PR curve for the same scores looks poor?

The false positive rate divides by all the negatives, a large number, so many false alarms still give a small rate. Precision divides by the flagged records, so the same false alarms weigh heavily.

Go deeper symbols, small recalls, practice, Python about 4 min

Reading the figure

The lazy model is the baseline of A1, applied to a yes-or-no question. The records are made-up. With three Ganges records, any recall is a rough estimate.

On the Ganges class, "Never flags" gives an accuracy of 99.5% and a recall of 0%. The model is useless for the one thing SharkCam must not miss, and accuracy cannot tell. Then choose "Flags all records". Recall jumps to 100% and precision drops to the base rate, 0.5%. Finally choose the logistic regression and move the threshold. At thresholds that find all three Ganges sharks the logistic regression has at least 4 false alarms and an accuracy of at most 99.3%, below the lazy model. A false alarm costs accuracy, and the lazy model makes none. At 0.30 it finds 2 of the 3 with 1 false alarm, and its accuracy is 99.7%.

When the positives are rare, read the PR curve and compare it with the dashed base-rate line (Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015).

Switch to the hammerhead class, where 57 positives give a smoother curve. The same effect appears in a milder form, with a lazy accuracy of 90.5%. With only three Ganges records, recall can take only four values: 0%, 33%, 67% or 100%. Its 95% interval is wide: finding 2 of 3 gives an interval from 21% to 94% (0.7). Three Ganges records are too few to show how well the model finds Ganges sharks. They show only that the lazy model finds none.

Symbols

\[ \text{accuracy of the lazy model} = 1 - \frac{n_{+}}{n} \qquad \text{random flagging: precision} = \frac{n_{+}}{n} \]

  • \(n_{+}\) is the number of positive records and \(n\) the number of all records. For the Ganges class \(n_{+}/n = 3/600 = 0.005\), so the lazy accuracy is 99.5%.
  • Any model should beat these two baselines on the measure that matters. The first baseline is the lazy accuracy. The second is the dashed line in the PR plot.

How well can a small recall be known?

Suppose a detector finds 27 of 30 rare animals. The recall is 90%, and the Wilson interval (defined in Subgroup analysis, later in this chapter) runs from 74% to 96.5%. Even 30 positives leave an interval about 22 points wide. With 3 positives, finding 2 gives 21% to 94%. To collect 30 Ganges sharks at a base rate of 0.5%, you need 6,000 records:

30positives wanted÷0.005base rate of the Ganges shark=6,000records to collect

Cross-validation meets the same limit. Five stratified folds deal three Ganges sharks into three of the folds, one apiece. The other two folds have no Ganges shark, and recall there is 0 ÷ 0. So collect the out-of-fold scores of all folds first, and compute the recall once on the pooled scores, as the figure does.

In practice

In practice, a model for a rare class is often trained with class weights or with extra copies of the rare records, so that training does not ignore them. That changes training only. Keep the evaluation set at the true mix, and choose the threshold on validation data, because reweighted scores are no longer probabilities.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Put the lazy baseline beside any measure you report. It takes one line: the share of the majority class, or zero recall. The same habit helped in the results table of 0.8, where the tree scored 80.2% and never found a Ganges shark.

In Python

import numpy as np

y = np.zeros(600, dtype=int)
y[:3] = 1                           # 3 Ganges sharks among 600 made-up records
pred = np.zeros(600, dtype=int)     # the lazy model never says "Ganges"

print("accuracy:", (pred == y).mean())
print("recall:  ", pred[y == 1].mean())

p, r = y.mean(), 1.0                # flag all records: recall 1
print("flag all: precision", p, " recall", r, " F1", round(2 * p * r / (p + r), 4))
accuracy: 0.995
recall:   0.0
flag all: precision 0.005  recall 1.0  F1 0.01

More questions

You want about 20 positives in a validation set, and the class is 0.5% of the records. How many records do you need?

At 0.5%, 20 positives need 20 ÷ 0.005 = 4,000 records. The made-up table has 600, so it is far too small for a reliable estimate of Ganges recall.

Base rates in screening

Guess first. At threshold 0.5, with out-of-fold scores for the 768 women in the Pima sample, the clinic model finds 57% of the women with diabetes and clears 88% of those without. Of the women it flags, 71% have diabetes. In a town where 10 in 100 women have diabetes, is a flagged woman more likely, equally likely or less likely to have it?

Screening tests people without symptoms to find the few who need a closer look. The model's sensitivity (recall) is the share of women with diabetes whom it flags, and its specificity is the share of women without diabetes whom it clears (does not flag). Precision (positive predictive value) depends on the prevalence (the base rate), the share of the women tested who have diabetes. The clinic model is a logistic regression on the Pima data, a published dataset of 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, not data from Mumbai. The Mumbai clinic is imagined.

  1. Circles are 1,000 women: coral has diabetes, navy does not, filled means flagged. Press "A town at 10% (made up)", then "A town at 2% (made up)". Sensitivity and specificity stay the same. The share of flagged women with diabetes falls from 71% to 34% and then to 8.3%. That is 11 of 133 flagged women after the figure rounds counts to whole women; without rounding it is 8.6%.
Where the model is used
has diabetes, flagged (TP)has diabetes, missed (FN)no diabetes, flagged (FP)no diabetes, cleared (TN)

With sensitivity (57%) and specificity (88%) fixed, the share of flagged women who have diabetes falls from 71% to 34% at 10% prevalence and to 8.3% at 2%.

How it works

Take a made-up town where 10 in 100 women have diabetes. Of 1,000 women, 100 are sick and 900 are not. The model flags 100 × 0.571 = 57 of the sick women (TP) and 900 × 0.124 = 112 of the healthy women (FP), because 0.124 is 1 minus the specificity 0.876.

57TP: 100 sick × 0.571÷169TP + FP: 57 + 112 (900 healthy × 0.124)=34%of flagged women have diabetes

In symbols, with sensitivity sens, specificity spec and prevalence p, the precision is sens × p ÷ (sens × p + (1 − spec) × (1 − p)). The top is TP per woman and the bottom adds FP per woman, so this is Bayes' rule with the model's own numbers. Bayes' rule turns sensitivity, specificity and prevalence into precision.

Common belief. A good test is good wherever it is used.

Why it fails. Sensitivity and specificity are measured on a sample with a given mix of sick and healthy people, and precision depends on that mix. In a town with a different mix the precision therefore changes, even though the model does not.

Better account. Report sensitivity and specificity, and work out the precision for the place of use with that place's prevalence, after checking that sensitivity and specificity still apply there.

Quick quiz

A screening model has sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%. At 1% prevalence, what share of flagged people have the condition?

Per 1,000 people, 10 are sick and 9 of them are flagged. Of the 990 healthy, 99 are flagged. Precision is \(9/(9+99) = 8.3\%\).

Does moving the threshold change the model's precision in the clinic? Does it change the prevalence?

It changes sensitivity and specificity, so it changes precision. It does not change the prevalence, which describes the women, not the model.

Go deeper data note, symbols, 2% town, practice about 4 min

About the data

The clinic is a story. The data are a published dataset: it has 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, all aged 21 or older (Smith et al., 1988). It does not come from Mumbai or from India. The model is a logistic regression on six of the measurements, scored out of fold.

Reading the figure

A circle is a woman. The coral circles have diabetes and the navy ones do not. A filled circle means the model flagged her. Slide the prevalence down. The coral share falls, and the share of filled circles that are coral shrinks. The number of navy filled circles (false alarms) rises slowly, from 81 per 1,000 women in the Pima sample to 112 at 10% and 122 at 2%. The false alarms come from the many women without diabetes, who are flagged at a rate of 12% whatever the prevalence. This is the Bayes calculation of 0.7, written with the confusion matrix: TP grows with the number of sick women and FP with the number of healthy women.

The practical consequence is for the person who gets a flag. At 2% prevalence, about 9 in 100 flagged women have diabetes, and the other 91 are sent for follow-up although they do not have diabetes. Screening can remain worthwhile at a low precision if the follow-up test can handle the false alarms. The clinic therefore needs to know the number and to design the follow-up for a high share of false alarms. Avoid telling a flagged woman that the model is 88% right about her. The model also assumes its sensitivity and specificity still apply in the new population. The lesson I drew in my diabetes screening project is that a model trained on one population may not suit another. The next section checks that assumption inside the data you have.

Symbols

\[ \text{precision} = \frac{\mathrm{sens}\cdot p}{\mathrm{sens}\cdot p + (1-\mathrm{spec})(1-p)} \]

  • sens is the sensitivity and spec the specificity of the model. \(p\) is the prevalence where the model is used.
  • The top is TP per woman (sens times \(p\)). The bottom adds FP per woman (1 minus spec, times the healthy share \(1-p\)). It is Bayes' rule from 0.7 with the model's own numbers.

A second case: the town at 2%

In the town with 2% prevalence, screen 1,000 women. Twenty have diabetes and 980 do not. The model finds 57.1% of the 20, so 11.4 are flagged. It flags 12.4% of the 980 healthy women, so 121.5 are flagged. The flagged group has 132.9 women, and 11.4 of them have diabetes:

11.4TP: 20 × 0.571÷132.9TP + FP: 11.4 + 121.5 (980 × 0.124)=8.6%of flagged women have diabetes

That is about 12 flagged women for one woman found. The women the model clears are 99.0% healthy. The lazy answer, that nobody has diabetes, is already right for 98%. At this prevalence a clear result adds little.

There is a shortcut in odds (A3). A flag multiplies the odds of diabetes by sensitivity over (1 minus specificity), here 0.571 / 0.124 = 4.6. At 2% the odds are 2 to 98, or 0.0204. After a flag they are 0.0204 × 4.6 = 0.094, a chance of 0.094 / 1.094 = 8.6%. The multiplier belongs to the model. The starting odds belong to the town.

In practice

In practice, plan the follow-up for the false alarms before you start. Screening 10,000 women at 2% gives 200 with diabetes, of whom about 114 are flagged, and about 1,215 false alarms. The follow-up clinic must be able to see about 1,330 women to find 114.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a paper or a test set was built by choosing equal numbers of sick and healthy people, its precision is for a 50% prevalence. Ask what the prevalence is where you will deploy, then recompute precision from sensitivity and specificity. Never read precision from a test set whose class balance somebody chose.

In Python

# sensitivity and specificity of the model at threshold 0.5
sens, spec = 0.571, 0.876

for prevalence in [0.349, 0.10, 0.02]:
    tp = sens * prevalence                  # per woman screened
    fp = (1 - spec) * (1 - prevalence)
    print(f"prevalence {prevalence:5.1%}: precision {tp / (tp + fp):.1%}")
prevalence 34.9%: precision 71.2%
prevalence 10.0%: precision 33.8%
prevalence  2.0%: precision 8.6%

More questions

A test set is built with 50% women who have diabetes and 50% who do not. With sensitivity 0.571 and specificity 0.876, what is the precision on it?

Per woman screened, TP = 0.5 × 0.571 = 0.2855 and FP = 0.5 × 0.124 = 0.062. Precision is 0.2855 / 0.3475 = 82%. That is far above the 9% to 34% of the towns, and it comes from the way the test set was built.

Subgroup analysis

Guess first. At a threshold of 0.5, the model of the last section, fitted to Pima women in the United States, finds 57% of the women with diabetes overall. Do you expect about 57% in women aged 21 to 29, and in women aged 50 and over?

A subgroup is part of the data picked out by one column, such as an age band. Subgroup analysis computes the same measures inside the subgroups at one threshold. An overall measure averages over the groups, so it can hide a group for whom the model works much worse. A 95% interval is a range, computed from the counts, that would contain the true value in about 95 of 100 samples. It is wide when few women lie behind it.

  1. Teal circles are sensitivity and navy diamonds specificity, with 95% intervals, for four age bands and all women. The circles rise and the diamonds fall with age, and the table under the plot gives the counts behind the dots.
  2. Choose "The 154 held-out women" (left out of the fitting): the intervals widen. The band of 50 and over has 7 of 7 women with diabetes found. In the boxes below, its plain interval is 100% to 100% and its Wilson interval 65% to 100%.
Women
sensitivity (circle)specificity (diamond)
Show the working for

At one threshold of 0.5, sensitivity rises from 46% for women aged 21 to 29 to 79% for women aged 50 and over, and specificity falls from 94% to 65%.

How it works

Take the 154 held-out women. The band of 50 and over has 7 women with diabetes, and the model finds all 7, so its sensitivity is 100%. The plain interval \(\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\), where \(\hat p\) is the observed share, \(n\) the number of women behind it and 1.96 the multiplier for a 95% interval, then has width zero.

7 of 7sensitivity in the oldest held-out group→100% to 100%plain: 1 ± 1.96 × 065% to 100%Wilson interval

The Wilson interval, another 95% interval (formula in the fold), stays inside 0% to 100% and does not have width zero at 7 of 7, so a small subgroup needs its counts and a Wilson interval. Of all 768 women, scored out of fold, 268 have diabetes. The model finds 34 of the 43 in the oldest band (79.1%, interval 64.8% to 88.6%) and 39 of the 84 in the youngest (46.4%, interval 36.2% to 57.0%). These intervals do not overlap, so the gap of about 33 points is unlikely to be chance.

Common belief. If the overall accuracy is good, the model works for all groups.

Why it fails. An overall measure is an average dominated by the largest group. A small group can have a much lower sensitivity or specificity (here 65% specificity for women aged 50 and over, against 88% overall) while the overall number moves little.

Better account. Compute the same measures inside the groups, show the counts and intervals, and compare them at the threshold you will use.

Quick quiz

A group has 4 women with diabetes and the model finds 4. Is the model perfect for that group?

Not on this evidence. Four cases are too few to show that. With 7 of 7 the Wilson interval already runs from 65% to 100%, and with 4 of 4 it is wider, about 51% to 100%.

Why is the overall sensitivity (57%) nearer to the youngest band's (46%) than to the oldest band's (79%)?

The overall sensitivity averages the band values, weighted by the number of women with diabetes in a band (84 in the youngest, 43 in the oldest). So the youngest band pulls it harder.

Go deeper symbols, counts, practice, Python about 5 min

Reading the figure

This is the kind of check I ran in my diabetes screening project, where I checked results across demographic subgroups for bias. Here the groups are age bands, and the predictions are those of the last section. The dots are sensitivity (circles) and specificity (diamonds), and the bars are 95% intervals. Under the plot, the table gives the counts behind the dots. Look at the table first. The youngest group has 396 women, over half the data, and 312 of the 500 women without diabetes, so the overall specificity is mostly that of women aged 21 to 29.

The model treats the groups differently at one threshold. It flags 15% of women aged 21 to 29 and 56% of those aged 50 and over. Diabetes is more common in the three older groups (46%, 55% and 48%) than in the youngest (21%). Age is one of the model's inputs, so a likely reason is that the older groups get higher scores. At the same threshold, the model misses more of the younger women who have diabetes and raises more false alarms for the older women who do not. Neither gap is a mistake of arithmetic, and a clinic would want to know both.

The intervals for the older groups are wider than those of the youngest, because fewer women lie behind them. The difference is largest for specificity: 51% to 77% for women aged 50 and over, against 90% to 96% for women aged 21 to 29.

Among the 154 held-out women the intervals widen. Two groups whose intervals do not overlap are likely to differ, and if the intervals overlap, the counts do not settle the question. Even a gap with no overlap is weak evidence when the groups were chosen after the fact from many possible splits. Woman A, the 28-year-old with glucose 158 who has diabetes, is in the youngest group, where the model misses more cases. At 0.5 she is found.

Symbols

\[ \frac{\hat{p} + \dfrac{z^2}{2n} \;\pm\; z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \dfrac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \dfrac{z^2}{n}} \qquad z = 1.96 \]

  • \(\hat{p}\) is the observed share (sensitivity or specificity in the group) and \(n\) the number of women it is computed on: those with diabetes for sensitivity, those without for specificity.
  • The plain interval \(\hat{p} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\) from 0.7 fails when \(n\) is small or \(\hat{p}\) is near 0 or 1. The formula above (Wilson, 1927) stays inside 0 and 1 and does not collapse to zero width at 100%.

Counts behind the bands

Counts from the cross-validated predictions: the youngest group has 84 women with diabetes, and the model finds 39. The sensitivity is 39/84 = 46.4%. The plain interval uses the standard error \(\sqrt{0.464 \times 0.536/84} = 0.054\) and gives 46.4% plus or minus 10.7 points, from 35.8% to 57.1%. The Wilson interval gives 36.2% to 57.0%. With 84 women and a share near one half, the two agree. They differ in the corners, near 0% and 100%.

The group aged 40 to 49 (40 of 65, 61.5%, interval 49% to 72%) overlaps the oldest group's interval, so these counts do not separate those two clearly.

In practice

In practice, pick the groups before you look at the results, and report all of them. A 95% interval misses the truth one time in 20, so across 20 subgroup comparisons you should expect about one false gap. A group with fewer than about 30 positives gives a wide interval: 15 of 30 is 50%, with an interval from 33% to 67%. Print the counts beside the measures.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When a group looks worse, check its size before you draw a conclusion about it. Then check its base rate and whether the column that defines the group is an input of the model. A gap in sensitivity with a different base rate is not the same finding as a gap in AUC. The fairness chapter (F1) returns to what a fair model means.

In Python

import numpy as np

# 12 made-up women, only to show the code
age = np.array([24, 27, 33, 45, 52, 61, 29, 38, 55, 23, 41, 66])
y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1])    # has diabetes
score = np.array([.4, .7, .2, .8, .9, .6, .1, .5, .7, .3, .45, .95])
flag = score >= 0.5

for name, lo, hi in [("under 40", 0, 39), ("40 and over", 40, 200)]:
    m = (age >= lo) & (age <= hi)
    sick = m & (y == 1)
    found = (flag & sick).sum()
    print(f"{name:12s}: women {m.sum()}, with diabetes {sick.sum()}, found {found}")
under 40    : women 6, with diabetes 3, found 2
40 and over : women 6, with diabetes 5, found 4

Terms

A disparity is a gap between the measures of two groups. The 95% interval is explained in 0.7.

More questions

In the 154 held-out women, the youngest group has 18 with diabetes and the model finds 7. Does that conflict with the 46% from cross-validation?

No. The model finds 39% (7 of 18), with a Wilson interval of 20% to 61%, and 46% lies inside it. Eighteen women cannot separate the two figures.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A detector gets TP = 36, FP = 12, FN = 24 and TN = 928 on 1,000 records. Find its accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1. Then find the accuracy of the lazy model on the same records and say what the comparison tells you.

    Hint

    The lazy model says "negative" for all records, so it is right for the records that are not positive. Count them from the matrix: positives are TP + FN.

  2. theory Show that \(F_1 = 2\,TP/(2\,TP + FP + FN)\) equals the harmonic mean \(2PR/(P+R)\) of precision \(P\) and recall \(R\). Then find \(F_1\) for a detector with precision 1.00 and recall 0.02, and compare it with the plain average.

    Hint

    Write \(P = TP/(TP+FP)\) and \(R = TP/(TP+FN)\), then bring \(2PR/(P+R)\) over a common denominator.

  3. theory Three hammerheads score 0.9, 0.6 and 0.4. Four other sharks score 0.7, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. Count the pairs in which the hammerhead scores higher and give the AUC. Then list the (FPR, TPR) points of the ROC curve as the threshold falls through the seven scores.

    Hint

    There are \(3 \times 4 = 12\) pairs. As the threshold passes a score, move up by 1/3 if the record is a hammerhead and right by 1/4 if it is another shark.

  4. theory A missed hammerhead costs \(c_{FN}\) and a false alarm costs \(c_{FP}\). For a record whose probability of being a hammerhead is \(p\), write the expected cost of flagging it and of not flagging it. Show that flagging is cheaper when \(p \ge c_{FP}/(c_{FP}+c_{FN})\). What threshold does a cost ratio of 8 to 1 give?

    Hint

    If you flag, you pay \(c_{FP}\) with probability \(1-p\). If you do not, you pay \(c_{FN}\) with probability \(p\).

Practice

  1. practice Build a hammerhead detector on the catch table (data/sharks/catch.csv in the primer's data folder). Use log length, log weight, log girth, depth and temperature as features and a logistic regression as the model. Compare three AUC values: on the validation set and on the test set of a stratified 60/20/20 split, and the 5-fold cross-validated AUC. Repeat with three seeds. Which of the three is steadiest, and why?

    Hint

    train_test_split(..., stratify=y) twice gives three sets. cross_val_predict(..., method="decision_function") returns out-of-fold scores for roc_auc_score.

  2. practice Load data/clinic/pima.json. Train an XGBoost model on the 614 training women (test = 0), with 100 trees, depth 3, learning rate 0.01 and seed 42. Score the 154 held-out women. Report accuracy, the accuracy of the lazy model, sensitivity and specificity at a threshold of 0.5. Is the gain over the lazy model large relative to the standard error of the score?

  3. practice Make a leak and measure it. Make three copies of the rows of the Pima women and add a little noise to Glucose, BMI and Age. Split the rows at random, fit a decision tree with no depth limit and record the test accuracy. Then split by woman (all three copies together) and record it again. How large is the gap, and what does a logistic regression do on the same two splits?

    Hint

    GroupShuffleSplit keeps all rows with the same group number together.

  4. practice Subgroups by BMI. Take out-of-fold scores for the 768 women from a cross-validated logistic regression. Split the women into BMI under 30 and 30 or over, leaving out the 11 whose BMI was not measured. Compute sensitivity and specificity at 0.5 with a Wilson interval for both groups. Do the intervals overlap?

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam will run on dives off Mumbai in the monsoon, when the water is murkier than in the dives used for training. Design the test of its hammerhead detector. What is the unit you split on? What do you report, and with what interval? Who chooses the threshold, and from which data?

  2. open A clinic in Mumbai wants to use a diabetes model trained on the Pima data. List what you would measure before it goes live, on whom, and what result would make you advise against using it. What would you say to a woman who is flagged?

  3. open The crew wants to claim that the detector "finds Ganges sharks". You have three Ganges records, and the detector found two of them. What can you claim, what can you not, and what data would you collect to firm it up? Would you choose accuracy, AUC or something else to track, and why?

Full solutions are kept off the page. Try the exercises before you look at the solutions.

Come back later

Answer these after two days, and again after a week. Say the answer aloud or write it down before you open it.

A model gets 121 of 154 held-out women right (78.6%). Use the standard error formula to give a 95% interval. Can you tell it apart from a second model that scores 80.5% on the same women? (0.7)

The standard error is \(\sqrt{0.786 \times 0.214/154} = 0.033\), so the interval is 78.6% plus or minus 6.5 points, from 72.1% to 85.1%. A model at 80.5% lies well inside it, so the two scores do not differ clearly. Compare the models on the same women with a paired test, as in 0.7.

In the polynomial figure the best degree was about 3, because weight grows like length cubed. What degree would you expect to work best if you fitted the logarithm of weight to the logarithm of length, and why? (A2)

Degree 1. Taking logs turns \(W = aL^b\) into \(\log W = \log a + b \log L\), a straight line. The flexibility a cubic gave in the original units is already built into the log-log scale.

In 0.8 the depth-3 tree scores 80.2% on the species table, and its confusion matrix has one hammerhead labelled "Ganges" and no true Ganges found. What is its accuracy on the yes-or-no question "is this a Ganges shark?", and how does it compare with the lazy model? (0.8)

It makes 3 misses and 1 false alarm, so 596 of 600 calls are right: 99.3%. The lazy model gets 597 of 600, 99.5%, so on accuracy the tree is slightly worse and finds no Ganges shark either.

  1. Saito, T. and Rehmsmeier, M. (2015). The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets. PLoS ONE, 10(3), e0118432. journals.plos.org
  2. Fawcett, T. (2006). An introduction to ROC analysis. Pattern Recognition Letters, 27(8), 861–874. doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2005.10.010
  3. Hanley, J. A. and McNeil, B. J. (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143(1), 29–36. The paper shows that the area is the probability that a randomly chosen positive is ranked above a randomly chosen negative.
  4. Wilson, E. B. (1927). Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 22(158), 209–212. doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1927.10502953
  5. Kaufman, S., Rosset, S., Perlich, C. and Stitelman, O. (2012). Leakage in data mining: formulation, detection, and avoidance. ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data, 6(4), article 15. doi.org/10.1145/2382577.2382579
  6. scikit-learn documentation. Common pitfalls and recommended practices (the data leakage section has an example in which choosing columns before splitting turns random labels into a 0.76 score) and Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance.
  7. Smith, J. W., Everhart, J. E., Dickson, W. C., Knowler, W. C. and Johannes, R. S. (1988). Using the ADAP learning algorithm to forecast the onset of diabetes mellitus. Proceedings of the Annual Symposium on Computer Application in Medical Care, 261–265. The first description of the Pima data used in the clinic sections. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

The shark records, the frames and the filler readings are made up. The clinic is a story, and the data in it are the published Pima records (768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States), not data from Mumbai. Results for the Pima women follow the 80/20 split of my diabetes screening project. Species facts come from the primer's data notes.
